svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling maximum instance lifetime. The setting specifies the maximum amount of time in seconds that an instance can be in service before it is terminated and replaced, and AWS names internal security policies and external compliance controls as the common use case. The minimum value is 86,400 seconds, one day, and a value of 0 clears a previously set value; the setting applies to all current and future instances in the group. It cannot be set when creating a group in the console, only by editing the group afterwards or through the CLI and API. Replacement pacing is adaptive rather than configurable: Auto Scaling usually replaces instances one at a time with a pause between replacements, but if the specified lifetime does not provide enough time to replace each instance individually it must replace more than one at a time, and several instances might be replaced at once by up to 10 percent of the current capacity of the group. Instances are not guaranteed to be replaced only at the end of their maximum duration, and Auto Scaling might need to start replacing instances immediately after the parameter is updated, in order to avoid replacing all instances at the same time. Two documented conditions mean an instance does not observe the limit. With instance scale-in protection enabled, Auto Scaling will not terminate the instance even if it has reached its maximum instance lifetime, and the same documentation recommends scale-in protection as a way to avoid replacing too many instances at once. And when there is only one instance in the group, the feature can result in an outage, because by default Auto Scaling creates a scaling activity to terminate the instance and then terminates it, launching a replacement while the instance is terminating; an instance maintenance policy changes this to launch before terminating. Replacement also acts as a deploy: whenever an earlier instance is replaced the new instance uses the launch template or launch configuration currently associated with the group, so if that template specifies the AMI ID of a different version of the application, that version is deployed automatically.
svg.title: A protected instance has no maximum lifetime
svg.text: A compliance clock with a documented opt-out.
“Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling will not terminate the instance even if it has reached its maximum instance
lifetime.”
The remedy and the loophole are the same setting
Replacing too fast? — “set a longer maximum instance lifetime or use instance scale-in protection”
Scale-in protected? — the instance is exempt, with no timeout and no escalation
A group can satisfy the setting and not the requirement behind it. Its configuration looks correct.
THE PACE IS NOT YOURS TO SET
Enough time per instance → one at a time,
with a pause between replacements
Not enough time → several at once, up to
10% of CURRENT capacity
So a scaled-out group replaces more at once.
SETTING IT CAN REPLACE TODAY
“Instances are not guaranteed to be replaced
only at the end of their maximum duration.”
“The reason for this behavior is to avoid
replacing all instances at the same time.”
Desynchronising an even-aged fleet starts now.
THE NUMBER
minimum 86,400 s (one day)
clear it set 0, not empty
scope all current and future
The console cannot set it when creating a group.
A GROUP OF ONE TAKES AN OUTAGE
Default order: terminate, then launch the
replacement while the old one terminates
With one instance, that gap has no capacity
Fix: an instance maintenance policy (post #125).
Replacement is a deploy, whether or not you meant one
“the new instance uses the launch template or launch configuration that is currently associated with
the Auto Scaling group” — so a different AMI “will be deployed automatically”.
No healthy-percentage controls, no rollback, no alarms, no status to poll. It is a property of the group, not an operation.
AWS names the use case: “internal security policies or external compliance controls”.
If you are using it as a control, monitor the instances it does not apply to — not the setting.
